data.name: Occurrence at JCR Outpost
data.detailed_description: A scientific mission in Antarctica goes awry when something is released from beneath the ice! Learn the secrets of JCR Outpost as you play a deadly game of cat and mouse with the randomly generated crew members. No two playthroughs will be the same as you discover who is friend, who is foe, and the truth behind JCR Outpost. Only you can solve the mystery of the Occurrence at JCR Outpost!

reviews.review:
[h1]What is Occurrence at J.C.R. Outpost?[/h1]

J.C.R. stands for James Clark Ross. He was a British naval officer in the 1800's. He is remembered for his exploration of the Arctic with his uncle, Sir John Ross, and Sir William Parry. Furthermore, he is also known for his own expedition to Antarctica. You play the role of the new administrator of the outpost which is located in the Antarctic. Your aim is to gather scientific samples from under the ice. However, it quickly becomes obvious that things are not as they seem. This is because there is an ancient monster in the midst with the intention of killing you. Therefore, you will quickly discover that the game is one of cat and mouse.

Due to the subject matter of the game older science fiction readers and viewers will immediately recall John Carpenter's, The Thing. It is also clear that the developer has drawn further inspiration from classic adventure games such as Maniac Mansion, Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders and many more. As I am an older gamer and was raised on these types of games I was immediately interested in finding out whether Brizzi's writing and game design skills could rekindle some of those memories.

[h1]A Retro Inspired Opening[/h1]

The welcome to the game was not a pleasing one for me. Windows 10 advised me that the game was not at my optimal settings. This was a little distressing as it is the first game to do that. As a result my first visit was to the settings screen. Thankfully I was able to change the game's settings to a full 1920 x 1080. The second thing that I noticed was the old midi style computer sounds.  However, given the style in which the game is firmly established - retro - it is somewhat unsurprising that these choices have been made. This is especially relevant when considering the marking of the game in both the graphics and sound department.

The quality of the graphics and the sound both leave a little to be desired. However, the emphasis on the game is in neither department so you theoretically could listen to a podcast and ignore the graphics for the most part. In fact, I would almost argue that the game may be better played with neither. Unfortunately, this may decrease the already niche audience for this game.

[h1]Choose Your Own Text Adventure[/h1]

The player does not move their character throughout the course of play. Instead, you are given a number of options in each room and you must choose one of them to advance the game. Therefore, the game is played almost entirely through the text related offerings. It almost feels that the graphics themselves are irrelevant. This, in some way, is a reminder to how games used to be like long ago. This further puts the game into the niche category. Because of this older gamers - or those who have played the classics - are much more likely to gain a positive experience from the game than younger whipper snappers who have not played this type of game before.

[h1]The Monster[/h1]

When you finally get to the stage where you release the monster it will hunt you down. It will also attack the other members of your crew. When it has successfully killed them it will shapeshift into them. You will only discover that the monster has shape shifted into one of your crew members when you are alone with that particular member. Once this occurs it shapeshifts back into its natural form and will attempt to devour you. This will be successful if you have nothing to defend yourself with. Therefore it is always important to find a weapon and to have one with you at all times. Thankfully unless you're being lazy this shouldn't be too much of a problem as there are a variety of weapons scattered throughout the game.

[h1]Short Playthroughs[/h1]

Once you come to grips with the gameplay and learn what is expected of you individual gameplays are about an hour long on average. The game has been designed to support multiple playthroughs. However, unless you are a perfect game achievement hunter, I do not believe that your gaming hunger will be satiated by playing this game multiple times. Therefore at the cost of $9.99 for a little over an hour's worth of entertainment the cost per hour ratio is sadly very high.

[h1]The Annoying Parts[/h1]

Unfortunately, the game has some very annoying components to it.

First, let's look at the rest, eat and bath component of the game. You are forced to do each act on an in-game hourly basis. I don't know about you but I certainly do not need to do each of them every hour. Because of this I argue that the game includes this feature to artificially increase both the difficulty of the game and the amount of time that it takes to complete a playthrough. Consequently, this is not a system that I support and wish that it was stripped from the game.

Secondly, and perhaps even more aggravating than this is the way in which the game coded the AI. If an NPC is standing where a door is the game removes the option of going through that door. No "excuse me dude, get out of my way I need to go through that door" option exists. When this happens you have to choose another option one of which is to do nothing but wait. I would argue that this feature is either bad coding or another example of the developer wanting to unnaturally increase the amount of time it takes to complete the game.

[h1]Is it Steamified?[/h1]

Partially. There are no trading cards but there are a set of 12 Steam achievements.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Some retro gamers may get a kick out of the style of the game. However, I find the gameplay in Occurrence at J.C.R. Outpost to be limited and the playthroughs short. There isn't enough of a lure for me to persist with the game through the first playthrough. Consequently, the $9.99 asking price is inflated when considered from a value perspective. The likelihood is that you will pick this up in a bundle at some point and unless trading cards are added to it it will remained unplayed. This is a shame as I really wanted to like this one.
